title: The Leap and the Pause: Nijinsky from Theatre Street to Montmartre
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Tiflis, a first son to the touring dancers
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The Setov opera company holds the season in Tiflis, and in its lodgings Eleonora Bereda bears Tomasz Nizynski a first son, Stanislav. Both parents are Polish dancers who live by contract and railway timetable, working the provincial circuit of the empire from the Caucasus to the Baltic and back. The children arrive in whichever city the season has reached. Stanislav is the first of three and the first to be shut away: institutionalized as a boy, he dies in a Petrograd hospital thirty years later, by which time his younger brother is also in a doctor's keeping.
suggested_refs: The Setov opera company's touring circuit through the southern provinces of the Russian Empire

stops.name: Kiev, the birth on tour
stops.date_confidence: day and month attested as 12 March; the year is disputed across sources between 1889 and 1890, and the gravestone's 1889 is itself contested
stops.campa: In Kiev, mid-season, the dancers' second son is born and named Waclaw Nizynski, the name Russia will render as Vaslav Nijinsky and Poland will keep claiming back. The family is Polish, the empire Russian, the christening is held at Warsaw, and the boy will spend his life called by whichever version of the name the country he is standing in prefers. Tomasz teaches him to jump before he can read. The elevation that Paris will one day treat as a miracle is a family trade, learned in wings and rehearsal rooms. No lodging address survives; the city is the whole of the record.
suggested_refs: Warsaw, where the infant was christened; the parish is not named in reachable sources

stops.name: Minsk, the birth of Bronislava
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The troupe passes through Minsk and a daughter is born there, Bronislava. She will train beside her brother on Theatre Street and dance in Diaghilev's company, and she is still making ballets decades after Vaslav has stopped speaking. Of the three children she is the one who carries the family craft into old age. Between Tiflis, Kiev and Minsk the three children are born a thousand miles apart in five years, and none of them in a town the parents chose. Eleonora keeps the accounts and the costumes; Tomasz dances the soloist's roles that the provincial theatres advertise.
suggested_refs: Bronislava Nijinska's memoirs of the family's touring years

stops.name: Odessa, the father as soloist
stops.date_confidence: period only: sources place Tomasz's Odessa seasons in the 1890s without fixing a year; January is a default
stops.campa: At the opera house on Odessa's Rishelievskaya Street, Tomasz Nizynski dances soloist roles for the Setov company while his sons watch from the wings. The children are used as stage children when a production wants them. The boy learns no syllabus here. He learns how a house sounds in the first minute, while it decides whether it will love a dancer. Within a few years the marriage will break and this circuit will close for the family, but the son already knows the inside of a theatre better than the inside of any home.
suggested_refs: The Odessa Opera and Ballet Theatre, where Tomasz Nizynski danced with the Setov company

stops.name: St Petersburg, the apartment on Mokhovaya Street
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month unrecorded and defaulted to January
stops.campa: Tomasz leaves the family for another woman and Eleonora takes the three children to St Petersburg, to an apartment on Mokhovaya Street, without a company or a contract, living on whatever teaching she can find. She has moved to the one city in the empire where a poor dancer's son can be made into an imperial one at the state's expense. The Imperial Ballet School feeds, clothes and boards its pupils. Everything that follows depends on her getting Vaslav through its doors, and she has three years to prepare him for the examination.
suggested_refs: 20 Mokhovaya Street, the family's first St Petersburg address

stops.name: St Petersburg, entry to the Imperial Ballet School
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the examination month is not fixed in reachable sources
stops.campa: At ten he is admitted to the Imperial Ballet School on Theatre Street, the state's own nursery for the Mariinsky stage, and passes into a boarded childhood of uniform, class, rehearsal and church. He studies under Sergei and Nikolai Legat, and under Enrico Cecchetti, whose method will follow him for the rest of his dancing life. The Russian boys nickname him the little Pole and beat him for it; the teachers watch the jump. In a system built to produce interchangeable excellence, he is marked almost at once as something the system did not plan for.
suggested_refs: The Imperial Theatre School on Theatre Street, later the Vaganova Academy

stops.name: St Petersburg, expelled over the catapult
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month not recorded in reachable sources
stops.campa: A schoolboy quarrel ends with a catapult, an injured classmate and Nijinsky expelled from the Imperial school. He is readmitted about a month later, the institution having decided it would rather keep the jump than the principle. The same year his brother Stanislav is committed for mental illness, and some accounts place a brief asylum stay of Vaslav's own around this period, a claim the sources neither develop nor drop. He returns to the classroom already carrying two facts the school cannot teach out of him: an extraordinary body and a family history.
suggested_refs: The disciplinary records of the Imperial Theatre School, St Petersburg

stops.name: Nevsky Prospect, the ninth of January
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The workers' procession comes toward the Winter Palace with petitions and icons, and the troops fire. Nijinsky is on Nevsky Prospect in the crowd that morning and is struck on the head, one wound among the thousands the day produces. He is fifteen, a pupil of the Tsar's own school, bleeding in the street where the Tsar's army has just settled a question of who the city belongs to. He goes back to class. The empire that trains him and pays him has shown him, in a single morning, what it is willing to do, and the school on Theatre Street continues its timetable unaltered.
suggested_refs: Bloody Sunday, 9 January 1905, and the crowds on Nevsky Prospect

stops.name: St Petersburg, graduation with top marks
stops.date_confidence: April 1907 in Wikipedia and Buckle; Encyclopedia.com gives 1908 instead, and the contradiction is not resolved
stops.campa: He leaves Theatre Street with the highest marks of his year after seven years inside it. Three years earlier Marius Petipa, the old man who made the Russian repertory, had picked the boy out for a principal role in a performance that in the end never took place, an appointment that exists only as a note in the record. The graduating dancer is short, thick-thighed, unremarkable in a corridor, and airborne in a way nobody can account for. The Imperial theatres take him immediately, and the Mariinsky stage is a fifteen-minute walk from the schoolroom.
suggested_refs: Marius Petipa's casting notes for the Imperial Ballet, 1904

stops.name: Mariinsky Theatre, coryphee at 780 roubles
stops.date_confidence: month and year attested; day defaulted to the first
stops.campa: He enters the Imperial Russian Ballet as a coryphee at seven hundred and eighty roubles a year, a salary for a promising boy, and is dancing principal work almost at once: La fille mal gardee, Le Pavillon d'Armide, the Bluebird pas de deux from The Sleeping Beauty. The Mariinsky is a court theatre. Its dancers are servants of the crown with pensions and rank, its repertory fixed, its costumes regulated. For four years he is its most talked-of young man, and by the time it dismisses him he will already have somewhere else to go.
suggested_refs: The Mariinsky Theatre's contract books for the 1907-1908 season

stops.name: St Petersburg, introduced to Diaghilev
stops.date_confidence: the introduction is placed in 1908 by Wikipedia, Ostwald and Buckle; one lens of the research pool gave 1909, which is the year of the Paris debut and not of the meeting. Venue unrecorded
stops.campa: Sergei Diaghilev, an impresario with no company, is introduced to the nineteen-year-old dancer, reportedly through Nijinsky's patron Prince Pavel Lvov. Diaghilev is thirty-six, ruthless about talent, and has already decided that what Russia can sell to Europe is not painting but spectacle. He takes the young man as lover, protege and instrument at once, and begins building a season in Paris around him. Nijinsky moves from an imperial contract into a private arrangement with a man who will make him famous within eighteen months and destroy him within five years.
suggested_refs: Prince Pavel Lvov, Nijinsky's patron and the reported intermediary
sources: Peter Ostwald, Vaslav Nijinsky: A Leap into Madness (1991)

stops.name: Theatre du Chatelet, the first Paris season
stops.date_confidence: the season opens in May 1909; the specific programme dates vary across the run
stops.campa: The Ballets Russes opens its first Paris season at the Chatelet with Le Pavillon d'Armide, Cleopatre and Le Festin, and the city decides overnight that it has been shown something it did not know existed. Nijinsky is twenty. Le Festin carries the Bluebird pas de deux with Tamara Karsavina, and the house behaves in a way Parisian houses are not supposed to behave. Within weeks he is the most famous male dancer in Europe, a category that had barely existed the season before, and Diaghilev has a company built on one body.
stops.quote: when those two came on, good Lord! I have never seen such a public. You would have thought their seats were on fire.
stops.quote_source: A Ballets Russes company courier on Nijinsky and Karsavina, Paris 1909; Richard Buckle, Diaghilev (1979), p. 143; also in Tamara Karsavina, Theatre Street
suggested_refs: The 1909 Ballets Russes programme for the Theatre du Chatelet

stops.name: Venice Lido, painted by Bakst
stops.date_confidence: year attested by the painting's caption; the month is a summer inference
stops.campa: Between seasons the company's inner circle takes the Adriatic, and on the Lido Leon Bakst paints Nijinsky, the designer setting down the dancer he has been dressing in silks and gold paint all spring. Nijinsky lodges with Diaghilev in Paris hotels through these years, the Daunou and then the Hollande, an arrangement at once professional and domestic that no one in the company discusses and no one fails to understand. He is being kept, dressed, taught languages and shown pictures, and he is being made into the thing Europe now expects to see.
suggested_refs: Leon Bakst's 1910 painting of Nijinsky at the Venice Lido

stops.name: Mariinsky Theatre, dismissed over the costume
stops.date_confidence: January 1911 attested; the day is not fixed. Sources disagree on which royal was present, Wikipedia naming the Tsarina Alexandra Feodorovna and Buckle the Dowager Empress Maria Feodorovna
stops.campa: He dances Giselle at the Mariinsky in Benois's costume, tights without the trunks the court requires over them, in front of the imperial box. The scandal is instant and the dismissal follows: the Imperial theatres will not keep a dancer who has embarrassed the palace. Whether the offence was planned by Diaghilev to free his star from a state contract, or was simply a young man's indifference to a rule, no source settles. The effect is the same. At twenty-one Nijinsky loses the pension, the rank and the country, and belongs entirely to a private company.
suggested_refs: Alexandre Benois's Giselle costume design, the object of the 1911 court scandal

stops.name: Salle Garnier, Monte Carlo, the rose
stops.date_confidence: Le Spectre de la Rose premieres in the Monte Carlo spring season of 1911; the company used the Salle Garnier as its winter workshop from 1911 to 1913
stops.campa: Monte Carlo is where the Ballets Russes builds what Paris later applauds, and in the Salle Garnier he first dances Le Spectre de la Rose: a girl asleep in a chair, a scent given a body, and an exit through the window that leaves the house in silence for a second before it starts shouting. The leap is caught by dressers in the wings. Within a year it is the most described physical act in Europe, argued over by people who never saw it. He is asked constantly how it is done, and gives the same answer.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Nijinsky; reaching print in Richard Wilbur's poem 'Grace' (1963). Original spoken context and date unestablished
suggested_refs: The Salle Garnier at Monte Carlo, winter workshop of the Ballets Russes

stops.name: Theatre du Chatelet, the puppet Petrushka
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Stravinsky's Petrushka opens at the Chatelet and Nijinsky dances the puppet: sawdust limbs, a face painted into permanent grief, a creature made by a showman for display and thrown away when it breaks. Fokine choreographs, Benois designs, Karsavina dances the Ballerina, and the audience watches a virtuoso spend an entire ballet refusing to be virtuosic. It is the role his admirers will name first for the rest of the century, and the one that gets set in bronze on his grave. Romola de Pulszky, who has not yet met him, is among those the company's effect works on.
stops.quote: An electric shock passed through the entire audience. Intoxicated, entranced, gasping for breath, we followed this superhuman being...
stops.quote_source: Romola Nijinsky, Nijinsky (1934), p. 4, describing her first sight of Nijinsky dancing with the Ballets Russes
suggested_refs: Benois's designs and Stravinsky's score for Petrushka, premiered 13 June 1911

stops.name: Theatre du Chatelet, the faun and the scarf
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: His first work as choreographer runs twelve minutes and moves in profile, the dancers held flat as figures on a vase, walking heel to toe against Debussy's score. At the end the faun lies down on the nymph's abandoned scarf and the body finishes the gesture. Le Figaro calls it filthy the next morning; police attend the second performance and take no action; Auguste Rodin defends it in print and is attacked for that in turn. The dancer everyone came to watch jump has just made a piece in which he barely leaves the ground, and the argument is about the last eight seconds of it.
suggested_refs: Rodin's published defence of L'Apres-midi d'un Faune, and the Figaro editorial it answered

stops.name: Theatre des Champs-Elysees, the game of tennis
stops.date_confidence: the pool attests 1913 and Paris; the May placement follows the same Champs-Elysees season and the day is not independently confirmed here
stops.campa: Jeux is set in a garden at dusk with a lost tennis ball, in sportswear, to Debussy: the first ballet to put modern people in modern clothes on a modern stage. Nijinsky plans it for three male dancers. Diaghilev reworks it into one man and two women before it is seen, and the piece that reaches the public is not the piece its choreographer designed. Paris finds it thin and forgets it in a fortnight. Two weeks later the same company opens something at the same address that nobody will be permitted to forget.
suggested_refs: Debussy's score for Jeux and the surviving notes on Nijinsky's original three-male scenario

stops.name: Theatre des Champs-Elysees, the Rite of Spring
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Stravinsky's music, Nijinsky's choreography and Nicholas Roerich's designs open together on the twenty-ninth of May in a hall four weeks old. The dancers stand pigeon-toed and heavy, heads dragged sideways, stamping against the beat toward a girl who will be danced to death. The house starts shouting before the first tableau ends. Nijinsky stands on a chair in the wings calling step numbers in Russian across a noise that swallows them while Monteux keeps the orchestra playing. Marcel Proust is placed in that audience by a report repeated for a century and never established.
stops.quote_source: Igor Stravinsky, An Autobiography (W. W. Norton, 1962 ed.), pp. 46-47, on the noise at the premiere
suggested_refs: Roerich's set and costume designs for Le Sacre du Printemps
Valentine Gross's sketches made in the theatre on the night

stops.name: Theatre Royal, Drury Lane, the Rite in London
stops.date_confidence: the date is that of The Times review of the London production; the London performances run through July 1913
stops.campa: The company brings Le Sacre du Printemps to London, where the audience declines to riot and the critics discuss it. The Times prints a long notice under the heading The Fusion of Music and Dancing, admiring how the elements hold together and complaining that the score has sold melody and harmony for rhythm. It is the last new work of his the London public sees him direct. Within a month he is at sea, and within six weeks the company that has commissioned every piece he has made will have dismissed him by telegram.
stops.quote: If M. Stravinsky had wished to be really primitive, he would have been wise to ... score his ballet for nothing but drums
stops.quote_source: The Times (London), 'The Fusion of Music and Dancing', 26 July 1913, p. 8
suggested_refs: The Times of 26 July 1913, p. 8, on the London Rite of Spring
sources: Peter Hill, Stravinsky: The Rite of Spring (2000)

stops.name: Cherbourg, sailing without Diaghilev
stops.date_confidence: August 1913 attested; sources differ on whether the company sailed from Cherbourg or Southampton, and the day is not fixed
stops.campa: The Ballets Russes sails for Argentina and Brazil without its director. Diaghilev will not cross open water, a superstition the company treats as law, and for the first time in five years Nijinsky travels with nobody who manages him. Aboard is Romola de Pulszky, a Hungarian officer's daughter and actress's daughter who has followed the company for a year and taken Cecchetti's classes to get near it. Cecchetti himself has told her what the man she is pursuing is. She has three weeks of ship, and no rival on board.
stops.quote: Beware, Nijinsky is like a sun that pours forth light but never warmth.
stops.quote_source: Enrico Cecchetti to Romola de Pulszky on Ballets Russes tour, c. 1912-1913; Romola Nijinsky, Nijinsky (1934), p. 13
suggested_refs: The 1913 South American tour manifest of the Ballets Russes
sources: Peter Ostwald, A Leap into Madness (1991)

stops.name: Rio de Janeiro, the port of call
stops.date_confidence: August 1913; the exact date of the Rio call is not fixed in reachable sources
stops.campa: The ship puts in at Rio de Janeiro on the way south. By now the courtship is conducted through an interpreter, since Nijinsky has no Hungarian and Romola almost no Russian, and the proposal itself will be made in French with a third person's help. He has spent his adult life inside an arrangement where another man handles money, contracts, hotels and language. On a boat in the South Atlantic that arrangement is three thousand miles away and cannot be consulted, and the decision belongs to him for the first time.
suggested_refs: The Ballets Russes 1913 crossing, Europe to Rio de Janeiro to Buenos Aires

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the marriage
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: They buy the wedding rings on arrival and marry in Buenos Aires on the tenth of September, days after landing, having known each other in any real sense for the length of an ocean crossing. The world press carries it within hours: the most famous dancer in Europe has married a Hungarian socialite nobody had heard of. In Europe one reader understands immediately what it means. The marriage is not a private event, because the man who made this career considers the career his, and considers Nijinsky his, and reads the announcement as theft.
suggested_refs: The Buenos Aires civil register for 10 September 1913; the exact church or registry is not named in reachable sources

stops.name: Teatro Colon, the last season as Diaghilev's dancer
stops.date_confidence: September 1913; individual performance dates within the engagement are not fixed here
stops.campa: The company plays its Buenos Aires engagement at the Teatro Colon, and Nijinsky dances the repertory that made him under a roof at the far end of the world. He is a married man of a few days, still the leading dancer of the Ballets Russes, and unaware for perhaps another fortnight that he no longer has an employer. It is the last stage on which he appears as what he has been since he was twenty: the centre of the most important company in Europe, dancing work built on his body by men who intended it for nobody else.
suggested_refs: The Teatro Colon's 1913 season programmes for the Ballets Russes

stops.name: Paris, the telegram of dismissal
stops.date_confidence: September 1913 attested; the exact date of the telegram is not fixed in reachable sources
stops.campa: Diaghilev learns of the marriage in Europe and answers with a telegram dismissing Nijinsky from the Ballets Russes. Five years of work end in a sentence: the partnership that produced Petrushka, Le Spectre de la Rose, the Faune, Jeux and the Rite is finished by wire, at distance, without a meeting. Nijinsky has no company, no repertory rights, no manager and no country he can return to, and has never in his life negotiated a contract. Every piece he has made belongs to the man who has just fired him.
suggested_refs: Diaghilev's 1913 correspondence on the dismissal, in the Ballets Russes papers

stops.name: Palace Theatre, London, his own company
stops.date_confidence: March 1914 attested for the eight-week season; the opening day is not fixed in reachable sources
stops.campa: He assembles a company of seventeen and books an eight-week season at the Palace, a music hall, sharing the bill with variety acts. He has no administrator, and it emerges that he cannot be one: rehearsals overrun, contracts fray, the season is cut short. Witnesses describe him nervous and distraught on the opening night. In the same weeks he attacks a stagehand who has flirted with Romola, and she records herself dumbfounded at a temper she has not seen before. Regular spectators who had followed him under Diaghilev come away saying something has gone.
stops.quote: he no longer danced like a god
stops.quote_source: Cyril W. Beaumont, Bookseller at the Ballet: Memoirs 1891-1929, p. 149, on the March 1914 Palace Theatre season
suggested_refs: The Palace Theatre's March 1914 playbills
Cyril Beaumont's memoirs of the Diaghilev ballet in London
sources: Cyril W. Beaumont, Bookseller at the Ballet

stops.name: Vienna, the birth of Kyra
stops.date_confidence: attested; some accounts wrongly place the birth in Budapest, where the family was interned weeks later
stops.campa: A daughter is born in Vienna and named Kyra. Her father is twenty-five, out of the company that made him, without engagements, and living on his wife's family. Nine days later a student shoots an archduke in Sarajevo. The dancer's private catastrophe of the previous autumn is about to be folded into a general one, and the passport he carries, issued by an empire he has not lived in since he was a boy on Theatre Street, is about to become the most important document in his life.
suggested_refs: Vienna civil register, 19 June 1914, birth of Kyra Nijinsky

stops.name: Budapest, house arrest at the Markus villa
stops.date_confidence: the internment runs from the outbreak of war in 1914 to early 1916; the day of confinement is not fixed
stops.campa: War is declared and Nijinsky, a Russian subject in Austria-Hungary, becomes an enemy alien in his mother-in-law's house. He is confined for nearly two years at the villa of Emilia Markus, the Hungarian actress whose daughter he married, watched by a family that regards him as a burden and a police category. There is no company, no class, no stage, and for a dancer in his twenties every month of it is taken out of the body. He fills the time with plans for a system of dance notation, and with nothing that can be performed.
suggested_refs: The villa of Emilia Markus in Budapest, place of Nijinsky's wartime internment

stops.name: New York, released into the American tour
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Diaghilev needs his name for an American tour he has already sold, and the release is worked through diplomatic channels and wartime prisoner exchange, the Spanish king and the American embassy both invoked. Nijinsky lands in New York on the fourth of April 1916 after twenty months of confinement. The two men meet again as employer and employee, with lawyers over unpaid salary between them. Whatever the partnership had been in Paris, it comes back as a business dispute conducted across an ocean by a company that needs a star it no longer controls.
suggested_refs: The diplomatic correspondence securing Nijinsky's 1916 release from Hungary

stops.name: Metropolitan Opera House, Till Eulenspiegel
stops.date_confidence: the autumn 1916 American season is attested; the day given here is the recorded Till Eulenspiegel premiere and is not independently confirmed in the pool
stops.campa: At the old Metropolitan Opera House on Broadway he dances and briefly directs the company for a reported sixty thousand dollars, the largest sum of his life. He makes Till Eulenspiegel there, to Strauss, in medieval costume: a trickster hanged at the end of his own ballet. It is his fourth and last work as a choreographer, made in a country that does not know his repertory, in a season assembled by an impresario who fired him three years earlier. No notation of it survives beyond fragments, and no film of him dancing anything survives at all.
suggested_refs: The old Metropolitan Opera House at 39th Street and Broadway
The 1916 Till Eulenspiegel designs by Robert Edmond Jones

stops.name: Petrograd, the death of Stanislav
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the month and the hospital are not named in reachable sources
stops.campa: In a Petrograd hospital, in the year the city stops being the imperial capital, Stanislav Nijinsky dies after most of a lifetime under institutional care. He was the eldest of the three touring children, committed as a boy, and effectively removed from the family's account of itself. His brother is on the other side of a war and a revolution and cannot come. Within two years a Zurich professor will apply to Vaslav the same word that closed over Stanislav in a St Petersburg ward when he was a boy.
suggested_refs: Petrograd hospital records for 1917; the institution is not identified in reachable sources

stops.name: Montevideo, the last performance
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the thirtieth of September, at a benefit for the Red Cross in Montevideo, Nijinsky dances in public for the last time in his life, accompanied by the pianist Arthur Rubinstein. He is twenty-eight. Nobody in the hall knows it is the last, including him. Ten years earlier he had walked out of a school on Theatre Street into the Mariinsky; the career that ends in a charity concert in Uruguay lasted from a Petersburg autumn to a South American spring, and produced four ballets and a body of roles that no film records.
suggested_refs: The Montevideo benefit programme of 30 September 1917

stops.name: St Moritz, the family settles in the mountains
stops.date_confidence: the move is placed in 1917; the month is not fixed in reachable sources
stops.campa: Company members have begun to notice the withdrawals, and the hours in which he says nothing at all. Romola takes him to St Moritz, to neutral country and mountain air, on the theory that rest will restore him. They stay two years in a rented villa above the lake with the child, the war grinding on beyond the passes. He walks, he draws, he tells the villagers he is a clown of God. What is happening to him has been given no name yet by anyone with the authority to give it one.
suggested_refs: The villa above St Moritz where the Nijinskys lived from 1917 to 1919

stops.name: Suvretta House, the last dance
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He announces a recital at the Suvretta House hotel and an invited audience assembles. He sits on a chair facing them without moving for half an hour. Then he lays out a cross on the floor in black and white velvet, stands at its head, and tells them he will dance them the war, the war they did not prevent, and dances until the room cannot look at him. Accounts of what exactly he did differ with the witness. All of them agree on the date, the cross, and the silence, and that it is the last time Vaslav Nijinsky dances in front of anyone.
suggested_refs: Suvretta House, St Moritz, site of the 19 January 1919 recital

stops.name: St Moritz, the six weeks of the notebooks
stops.date_confidence: the notebooks are written between January and early March 1919; the starting day is approximate
stops.campa: In roughly six weeks he fills four notebooks in pencil: on God, on meat and killing, on Diaghilev, on Romola, on his own body, addressed by turns to the deity and to an imagined public, with drawings of eyes in the margins because he feels watched. He writes down that he is afraid they will take him to a hospital. He is writing the only extended account of a great dancer's mind in his own hand, and he is writing it in the certainty that it will be used as evidence, which within weeks is exactly what happens.
stops.quote: People like eccentrics and they will therefore leave me alone, saying that I am a 'mad clown.'
stops.quote_source: The Diary of Vaslav Nijinsky, c. 1919; quoted in Peter F. Ostwald, Vaslav Nijinsky: A Leap into Madness (1991), ch. 8, p. 176
suggested_refs: The four St Moritz notebooks, 1919, with their marginal drawings of eyes
sources: Vaslav Nijinsky, The Diary of Vaslav Nijinsky (unexpurgated ed., Joan Acocella)

stops.name: Burgholzli, Zurich, the diagnosis
stops.date_confidence: the Zurich examination takes place in 1919; the day given here is approximate and the month is placed at the end of the diary period
stops.campa: Romola brings him to Zurich, to the Burgholzli, and Eugen Bleuler examines him. Bleuler is the man who coined the word schizophrenia eleven years earlier, and he applies it. Romola is told her husband is incurably insane and should be committed. The dancer understands what the interview is for; he had written down the fear of it in the notebooks a few weeks before. He is twenty-nine years old, and the professional opinion just recorded in Zurich will govern the remaining thirty-one years of his life without ever being revised.
suggested_refs: The Burgholzli clinic under Eugen Bleuler, and the 1919 case notes

stops.name: Bellevue Sanatorium, Kreuzlingen
stops.date_confidence: the transfer follows the 1919 Zurich diagnosis; the month is not fixed in reachable sources
stops.campa: He is transferred to Ludwig Binswanger's Bellevue at Kreuzlingen, on the German border, the most fashionable private asylum in Europe and the address of a long list of famous patients. Insulin comas, sedation, walks in the grounds. A second daughter, Tamara, is born in 1920 to a father who is a resident of a clinic. For most of the next thirty years he says very little to anyone, and the man Europe had watched more closely than any other body of his generation is watched now by orderlies and paid for by the sale of his own story.
suggested_refs: The Bellevue Sanatorium at Kreuzlingen under Ludwig Binswanger

stops.name: Sopron, moved away from the front
stops.date_confidence: the Sopron years are placed in the early to middle 1940s; no month or year is fixed in reachable sources, and January is a default
stops.campa: The second war finds them in Hungary, and Romola moves him west to Sopron, near the Austrian border, away from Budapest and the bombing. He is in his fifties, silent for the most part, cared for by his wife and by whoever else can be paid or persuaded. In 1936 she had published his notebooks in her own edited version, and the money from the book is part of what keeps them. He does not read it. Around him a continent repeats, on a larger scale, the war he had tried to dance to an audience of hotel guests in 1919.
suggested_refs: Sopron, western Hungary, where the Nijinskys spent the later war years

stops.name: Vienna, speech returns among the Russian soldiers
stops.date_confidence: 1945 attested; the month follows the Soviet occupation of Vienna and is not independently fixed
stops.campa: In occupied Vienna, Soviet soldiers are billeted around them and Nijinsky hears Russian spoken in the street for the first time in decades. He goes among them. He talks to them, and he dances for them, and after years of near silence the language of his childhood brings him back into speech. The men have no idea who the old Pole in the courtyard is. It is the one documented recovery in thirty years of illness. No clinic prescribed it. An army occupying a ruined city produced it.
suggested_refs: Accounts of Nijinsky among Soviet soldiers in Vienna, 1945

stops.name: Virginia Water, Surrey, the last house
stops.date_confidence: the move is placed in 1947; the month is not recorded and some accounts locate the residence slightly differently within Surrey
stops.campa: England takes them in at the end of the wandering, and the last years are spent at Virginia Water in Surrey, privately cared for. London had watched him at Covent Garden and at the Palace forty years earlier, and London dancers come out to Surrey to see him: the young of a new English ballet paying respects to a man who is, to them, a photograph that moves. He walks in the garden. He is occasionally persuaded to demonstrate a step, and those who see it write that the feet still know what to do.
suggested_refs: Virginia Water, Surrey, the Nijinskys' final residence

stops.name: London, death in the clinic
stops.date_confidence: attested; his age at death is sixty or sixty-one depending on which disputed birth year is used
stops.campa: He dies of kidney failure in a London clinic on the eighth of April 1950. He has outlived Diaghilev by twenty-one years, and his own dancing career and the empire that trained him by thirty-three each. The obituaries print the same handful of photographs, the faun in profile, the rose at the window, the puppet with its painted grief, because there is nothing else: not one foot of film of him dancing is known to survive, and the accounts say Diaghilev discouraged the cameras on the grounds that they would libel him.
suggested_refs: The 1950 obituary notices; the London clinic is not named in reachable sources

stops.name: Cimetiere de Montmartre, reinterred among dancers
stops.date_confidence: the reinterment is dated 1953; the month and day are not recorded in reachable sources
stops.campa: Three years after the London burial his remains are moved to Paris and laid in the Montmartre cemetery, near Auguste Vestris, near Theophile Gautier who invented Giselle, near Emma Livry who burned to death in her costume at nineteen. The city of his triumphs takes him back into a plot of dancers. Later a Russian group from Perm, without asking the family, adds a bronze of him seated as Petrushka: the broken puppet, on the grave, in perpetuity. The stone gives his birth year as 1889, which is one of the two years the sources offer.
suggested_refs: The Nijinsky grave at Montmartre with the Petrushka bronze by the Perm donors

stops.name: Hamburg, the ballets made about him
stops.date_confidence: Vaslav is created for Hamburg Ballet in 1979; the premiere day is not fixed in reachable sources
stops.campa: John Neumeier makes Vaslav for the Hamburg Ballet in 1979 and keeps returning to the subject for four decades, staging the diary, the Suvretta recital, the lost repertory, until his company is the principal keeper of the legend on stage. Maurice Bejart had already made Nijinsky, Clown of God in 1971, taking the phrase from the notebooks and building a martyrdom out of it. Herbert Ross films the story in 1980 with Alan Bates as Diaghilev. The man who left no film becomes a role that other dancers audition for.
suggested_refs: John Neumeier's Nijinsky cycle for the Hamburg Ballet, 1979 onward
Maurice Bejart, Nijinsky, Clown of God (1971)

stops.name: Teatr Wielki, Warsaw, the faun and the nymph in bronze
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Poland's first sculpture of him is unveiled in the foyer of the Grand Theatre in Warsaw, a bronze by Giennadij Jerszow showing Nijinsky and his sister Bronislava as the Faun and the Nymph. He was christened in this city and never worked in it. Russia trained him, France made him, Hungary interned him, Switzerland kept him and England buried him first, and the country whose language his parents spoke gets him a century later in metal, standing beside the sister who outlived him and went on making ballets after he stopped.
suggested_refs: Giennadij Jerszow's bronze of Nijinsky and Nijinska, Teatr Wielki, Warsaw, unveiled 11 June 2011
